text.p: The 10-year bond future ended sharply higher in heavy volume, powered by a U.S. dollar which drew strength from comments by Bundesbank council member Otmar Issing predicting a possible switch to U.S. assets at the start of European monetary union.

The dollar's advance helped the franc recover its poise after its recent battering following comments by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing urging a sharp devaluation of the unit against the dollar.
In late trade, the franc was trading at 3.3796 per mark, up more than a centime from its price late Monday of 3.3910.

Renewed hopes of interest rate easing by Germany and France early in 1997 following weak German industrial production data also boosted the market. News that industrial production fell 1.8 percent in October sent German debt prices soaring.

The Bundesbank, apparently seeking to douse the rate cut talk, pointed to statements earlier by its chief Hans Tietmeyer that rates would remain steady in the short term. Economists also noted German output figures are notoriously volatile.
After surging to a new contract high of 130.18, the notionnel lost some ground on profit-taking.

Dealers said there could be some consolidation on Wednesday but they did not expect any big losses and they said the market was still bullishly oriented. "The market is very solid and the outlook is good," said one analyst.
"I think the market may pause to catch its breath," said another analyst. "But we are well on the way to new records."
The benchmark 10-year OAT nearly reached 5.50, its lowest level ever and one analyst saw it reaching that level between now and the end of the year.
The franc's strength and the interest rate hopes propelled PIBOR to a contract high of 96.66 before it retreated slightly.
